title: Mastering LLM Inference Optimization From Theory to Cost Effective Deployment: Mark Moyou

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is serving trained LLMs in production, with extensive coverage of KV cache, quantization, inference engines (TRT-LLM, Triton, NIM), batching, parallelism, and latency/cost tradeoffs.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is serving trained LLMs in production, with extensive coverage of KV cache, quantization, inference engines (TRT-LLM, Triton, NIM), batching, parallelism, and latency/cost tradeoffs.

summary: Dr. Mark Moyou's talk builds foundational intuition for LLM inference workloads and then transitions into practical measurement, optimization, and deployment tooling. Moyou, an NVIDIA senior data scientist working primarily with retail clients, frames the challenge: LLM inference is not standard deep learning deployment, and cost is the primary barrier to scaling. He notes most organizations run hybrid setups combining big-box APIs with internally hosted or fine-tuned open-source models. The core explanation begins with what happens when a prompt reaches a GPU: text is tokenized using model-specific tokenizers, converted to token IDs, then to embedding vectors forming matrices. GPUs excel because they process matrices efficiently. The prefill stage computes the attention mechanism across the entire prompt per user. Generation proceeds one token at a time, with each generated token stored on the GPU as KV Cache, which Moyou identifies as a major cost driver. The attention mechanism uses query, key, and value matrices as actual model weights. Llama has 32 attention heads, each with its own KV Cache. A key mental model: parameters times two equals FP16 gigabyte memory on the GPU, so an 8B model in FP16 takes 16GB, leaving only 4GB on a 20GB GPU for KV Cache. The GPU holds only model weights or tokens—nothing else—so shrinking model size frees memory for tokens. Moyou covers performance measurement: time to first token measures attention mechanism processing quality, inter-token latencies track generation speed under load, and time to total generation measures end-to-end completion. He identifies four querying patterns—long input short output, long input long output, short input short output, and short input long output—each with different cost and performance implications. A 2D histogram of input versus output sequence lengths helps statistically determine max lengths for sizing optimized inference engines. The talk then covers deployment tooling: TRT-LLM is NVIDIA's model compilation package for LLMs on NVIDIA GPUs, producing engines compiled to specific GPU hardware that cannot be moved between GPUs. Triton is an open-source inference server written in C++ that hosts models across CPU, GPU, and multiple frameworks. NVIDIA Inference Microservices (NIM) provides pre-optimized configurations as an enterprise offering. Key optimization techniques include FP8 quantization (roughly halving model size with minimal accuracy loss), quantized KV Cache, paged KV Cache for better GPU memory management, in-flight batching that injects new requests immediately as others finish, and tensor parallelism (splitting models across GPUs within a node) versus pipeline parallelism (sequential processing across nodes). The future points toward FP4 on Blackwell GPUs. Moyou also introduces the concept of seasonal engines—different inference engines built for different querying patterns based on time-of-day traffic variations.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.summary: Moyou introduces himself as an NVIDIA senior data scientist working with retail clients on data processing, computer vision, and now LLM inference. He frames the talk around understanding the LLM inference workload, measuring production deployments, and controlling deployment costs. He mentions NVIDIA resources for benchmarking models.

sections.title: LLM Inference Workload Fundamentals
sections.summary: Explains what happens when a prompt reaches a GPU: tokenization, prefill stage computing attention on entire prompt per user, and one-token-at-a-time generation with tokens stored as KV Cache. Introduces the complexity of serving millions of concurrent users.

sections.title: Tokenization and Embedding Vectors
sections.summary: Details how text converts to token IDs using model-specific tokenizers, then to embedding vectors forming matrices. Notes tokens are sub-word units, not human words. Llama has 128,000 tokens. Explains why GPUs are suited: fast matrix processing.

sections.title: Attention Mechanism and Model Weights
sections.summary: Introduces the attention mechanism as relating tokens to determine importance for next-token prediction. Explains query, key, and value matrices as actual model weights used in matrix multiplication against input embeddings.

sections.title: KV Cache Value and GPU Memory Model
sections.summary: Explains KV Cache as the LLM's memory stored on the GPU. Without it, prior prompt processing would need recomputation. With it, generation only computes attention on the newest token against prior context. Llama has 32 attention heads each with separate KV caches. Introduces the mental model: parameters times two equals FP16 gigabytes, so an 8B model takes 16GB, leaving limited space for KV Cache.

sections.title: Performance Measurement Metrics
sections.summary: Covers time to first token (measures attention mechanism processing quality), inter-token latencies (tracks generation speed under load), and time to total generation. Explains ISL and OSL terminology. Notes that drift in inter-token latency under load indicates performance issues.

sections.title: Single Model per GPU and Querying Patterns
sections.summary: Contrasts standard multi-model GPU deployment with LLM inference where one model per GPU is typical, with remaining space for KV Cache. Identifies four querying patterns (long/short input x long/short output) as the most important slide for determining cost and performance. Long input long output is most costly.

sections.title: Inference Engine Sizing and Performance Analysis
sections.summary: Shows 2D histograms of input versus output sequence lengths for statistically determining max lengths to size optimized inference engines. References gen_perf open-source package for generating performance plots. Covers token-to-token latency analysis and time to first token versus input token count analysis, emphasizing minimal slope as a performance indicator.

sections.title: TRT-LLM, Triton, and NVIDIA Inference Microservices
sections.summary: Introduces Triton as an open-source C++ inference server hosting models across CPU, GPU, and frameworks including PyTorch and TensorFlow. Presents TRT-LLM as NVIDIA's model compilation package for LLMs on NVIDIA GPUs, producing GPU-specific engines. Introduces NVIDIA Inference Microservices (NIM) as an enterprise offering with pre-optimized model configurations. Highlights FP8 quantization benefits on Hopper and Ada Lovelace GPUs.

sections.title: Optimization Techniques and Parallelism
sections.summary: Covers in-flight batching (injecting new requests as existing ones finish), quantized KV Cache (shrinking KV Cache memory via different precision), paged KV Cache (better GPU memory management), and tensor parallelism (splitting model across GPUs within a node for reduced latency). Contrasts with pipeline parallelism for sequential multi-node processing. Mentions NVIDIA's 340B model designed for single H100 node FP8 inference.

sections.title: Future Directions and Q&A
sections.summary: Discusses the FP16 to FP8 to FP4 progression, with FP4 on Blackwell GPUs as the next major innovation. Covers Q&A on interpreting 2D histograms for engine sizing, introduces seasonal engines concept for time-of-day querying patterns, discusses LoRA adapter management strategies (typically one engine for all querying types), and addresses attention mechanism scaling challenges including Flash Attention and NV Link connecting 72 GPUs on Blackwell.
